title: DR1's hub ends with a "Review and submit" button a user can press at any point; the frontend replaces it with a "Check and submit" task row that stays shut until every other task is finished.

finding.frontend: The hub's last section is "6. Check and submit", holding a single row titled "Check and submit" with the hint "Check your answers before you submit the notification". It has no link and reads "Cannot start yet", and it stays that way until every task row is Completed, not applicable or optional (src/server/app/flow/section-status.js:11-15, consulted through the review section's gate in src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/flow/flow.js:81-84 and rendered at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/hub/controller.js:72-90). The only button on the page is "Return to dashboard" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/hub/template.njk:37-41), and the hub row is the interface's only route to the check-your-answers page, so there is no way to look over an unfinished notification.
finding.prototype: DR1's hub has no review task row at all. Below the task list sit two buttons, a primary "Review and submit" linking to /review-notification and a secondary "Return to dashboard" (app/views/notification-hub.html:81-92). The link is fixed, so it works from the first visit, and DR1 has a designed state for arriving there early: an incomplete review that names what is still outstanding and lists what must be done before the import.
finding.difference: Replace the blocked "Check and submit" row with a "Review and submit" button that is always available, and let the review page itself say what is missing rather than the hub refusing to open it. This depends on the review page tolerating an incomplete notification, which the review slice covers; the hub change is the section, the row and the button.
finding.falsifiedBy: A frontend hub with unfinished tasks that still offers a working route to the check-your-answers page.
finding.verification:
Opened the fe-hub, fe-hub-no-commodity, fe-hub-exit-details-blocked and dr1-notification-hub DOMs and the fe-hub and dr1 screenshots, and read hub/controller.js:70-91, flow/section-status.js:11-15, flow/gates.js:34-43, linear/flow/flow.js:81-86, hub/template.njk:37-41 and notification-hub.html:81-92. Ran the falsifier over all three frontend hub captures: in every one the Check and submit row is a bare
  • with no , and the only in the main content is "Return to dashboard" pointing at "/" — so no route to check-your-answers is offered anywhere on the page, including the fe-hub capture where ten of the eleven rows are open. Because this slice's danger is markup mistaken for behaviour I checked the route side as well and it does not undo the finding: the notification-view page is registered through `pageRoutes`, which attaches no gate, and `entryGuardTarget` only diverts a journey with no run record and no committed answers, so the page itself is unguarded — it is unlinked, not unreachable. Grepping for `notificationViewPage` finds it only in flow.js and its own controller, so the hub row is the sole route the interface offers, which is what the sentence claims. Narrowed the frontend slot's closing clause to say so explicitly. DR1's side is in the capture: `Review and submit` next to the secondary Return to dashboard, on a hub where every row still reads "To do", and the view hard-codes that href rather than deriving it. CORRECT.
finding.correction: Mis-stated rather than wrong. The frontend slot said "there is no way to look over the notification before it is complete"; the check-your-answers route carries no gate of its own — `pageRoutes` in shared/kit.js:137-150 attaches none and the entry guard only catches a never-entered journey — so the page is unlinked rather than unreachable. The user-facing claim is unaffected because the hub row is the only route the interface offers; the clause is reworded to name the route rather than the page.

relatedTo.why: both are the hub withholding a route the DR1 hub always offers

Two halves of one capability, named in each other's prose but unlinked until the duplicate sweep. Opening the route without the incomplete state gives a user a review page that calls every gap "Not provided"; building the incomplete state without this leaves it unreachable. Two findings, one release.
